BRIEF.CZ: No terrorism, sabotage, unrest or major transport disruption was confirmed in Czechia for 7-21 October; the Senate and municipal election cycle ended with a clear opposition win and no reported incidents. The country remains exposed to the regional hybrid-sabotage campaign against Ukraine-linked defence supply chains, but nothing in the window indicates an active threat; the first named autumn storm, Austin, is forecast to bring strong gusts over the weekend of 24-25 October. Travel to Prague and regional centres is routine.
BRIEF.GB: The UK's security picture is dominated by Iranian state-linked activity: the Fairford investigation moved on 20 October to National Security Act rearrests for assisting Iranian intelligence, a separate intrusion at RAF Molesworth is being handled under the same act, and MI5 warned on 13 October that Iran and Russia are stepping up hybrid campaigns. The national threat level has been Severe since April. No attack occurred in the window and daily business travel is unaffected, but US-linked military sites, Jewish community areas and Iranian-dissident venues carry elevated risk. The cost-of-living unrest seen in France, Belgium and Italy has not spread to Britain.
BRIEF.DE: Germany's state-threat environment remains layered: a Hamburg court confirmed Iranian direction of a plot against Jewish leaders, Bulgaria issued European arrest warrants on 19 October for two 19-year-old German nationals over the Starlink antenna arson near Sofia, and German police are holding four people over the Russian-attributed Polish Starlink arson. The Leipzig fence breach that raised sabotage fears turned out to be a learner driver, and the Nuremberg closure a radio fault, so the window produced alerts rather than attacks. For travellers the practical impact is sporadic airport delays and heightened security around Jewish and Israeli sites; the violent unrest in France and Italy has not spread to Germany.
BRIEF.SK: No terrorism, sabotage, violent protest or transport disruption was confirmed in Slovakia between 7 and 21 October. The risk is political: the Fico government's deepening engagement with Moscow, including the 26 October commission meeting, sustains a cycle of large but peaceful opposition protests, and the August foiled arson plot against a drone factory showed exposure to the regional sabotage campaign. Business travel to Bratislava and Košice is routine.
BRIEF.AT: Austria recorded no significant security incident in the window; the only notable event is the Vienna counter-espionage case, in which two Ukrainians remain in pre-trial custody (Austrian media report it has been extended to 20 November) after two Ukrainian journalists were briefly swept up and released. Vienna remains a hub for intelligence activity linked to the Ukraine war, but the threat to travellers is low. The pan-European cost-of-living unrest has not reached Austria.
BRIEF.BE: Belgium is the most exposed of the smaller core states to the French contagion: student-led unrest reached Francophone Belgium in early October and turned violent in Brussels and Liège on 17 October, while union action against the stalled federal budget disrupted the airport, rail and schools on 9 and 12 October. Budget talks collapsed again on 18 October and De Wever resumed bilateral negotiations on 19 October; several foreign governments have issued travel advisories for Belgian protests. Expect further Friday/weekend disruption in Brussels and the risk of new strike days while the budget remains unresolved.
BRIEF.IT: Italy has moved from routine strike disruption to sustained violent unrest: the 17-18 October riots in Milan, with clashes in Turin, Bologna, Brescia and Bergamo, injured more than 100 police, and the government responded on 20 October with 500 extra soldiers for Milan and an emergency decree creating new protest offences, while luxury retailers in the centre boarded up. Southern fuel and supply blockades by truckers add operational risk for road moves and regional logistics, with Calabrian hauliers striking until 27 October and the CGIL general strike set for 20 November. Plan movements away from city centres on Fridays and Saturdays and build fuel and routing contingencies for the south.
BRIEF.ES: Spain's immediate risk is environmental: Storm Adam killed at least four people in the Valencia region and Catalonia, alerts were lifted on 20 October and clean-up in Oliva, Pego and the Marina Alta will disrupt road travel for days, with orange warnings lingering in the Balearics. The 18 October Basque terrorism arrests, involving data on security forces and a suspected arms and explosives cache, are the first such case in years but appear contained. Social tension is elevated but protests over housing and living costs have stayed largely peaceful since the far-right clashes of 3 October, with the 29 November early election ahead; terrorism and crime indicators otherwise unchanged.
BRIEF.FR: France is the epicentre of the European unrest wave: a month-old student movement fused with cost-of-living anger on 17 October into nationwide rioting that left 997 police injured, 2,397 arrested and at least 3,000 shops looted, prompting the first big-city curfews in years, which were extended on 20 October and are to remain 'as long as necessary'. The government has admitted intelligence and policing failures and will use counter-terrorism military units in static roles for the next national protest day on Saturday 24 October, while unions have called a national strike for 5 November and 10-year bond yields hit a 24-year high. Risk stays high for at least two to three weeks; avoid central Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Lille on protest days and plan movements around curfew perimeters.
BRIEF.PL: Poland's window was front-loaded: a cluster of school stabbings that triggered nationwide school security operations, a credible threat against the prime minister with a cache of improvised explosives, and arrests in the Russian-attributed Starlink sabotage case, followed on 16 October by the detention of a 31-year-old Polish-Ukrainian reservist on an officer course in Łódź on spying suspicion. The last week has been quieter, but Siemoniak describes near-daily Russian subversion and the pattern of hybrid attacks on infrastructure supporting Ukraine keeps the baseline elevated. Warsaw remains fully workable.
BRIEF.NO: Norway remains a low-risk operating environment; the only in-window event affecting movement was the security operation around the 20 October Oslo talks between Zelensky, Witkoff, Store and Stubb, which passed without incident. The hybrid picture continues to tighten in the north, with the Coast Guard checking sanctioned Chinese heavy-lift vessels sheltering off Andøya and Norway's alignment with the EU's latest Russia sanctions package taking effect on 21 October, but none of this touches travellers. Expect continued friction with Russia over Arctic shipping and Svalbard with no change to travel advice.
BRIEF.FI: Finland is safe for travel and operations, but the south-eastern coast between Loviisa and the Russian border is subject to short-notice air and sea closures whenever Ukraine mounts large strikes on St Petersburg; Finnish media reported Defence Forces restrictions on 16, 17 and 18 October, lasting up to seven hours, with no drones crossing into Finland. No violence occurred in the window. The eastern land border remains closed to civilian traffic indefinitely, GNSS interference persists in the Gulf of Finland, and the government is building counter-drone capacity, most recently with €32m in EU funding for the Border Guard confirmed on 15 October.
BRIEF.EE: No significant security incident occurred on Estonian territory between 7 and 21 October 2026; the most recent notable event remains the August arson attack on Milrem Robotics in Tallinn, which Tallinn attributed to Russian special services on 29 September. In-window reporting is dominated by deterrence and resilience: NATO Secretary General Rutte's 14 October visit, Foreign Minister Tsahkna's 15 October warning that Russia will intensify hybrid attacks on critical infrastructure and defence firms, and nearly €32m in EU funding confirmed on 16 October for eastern-border drone surveillance. Travel to Tallinn is routine; vehicle traffic through the Narva crossing remains suspended and any onward travel into Russia carries serious detention risk.
BRIEF.RU: Russia's two principal cities remain under sustained Ukrainian drone attack: the 18 October assault on St Petersburg was the largest yet, killing one, injuring 15 and setting the city's oil terminal ablaze, while Reuters reported a 15 October strike that set fire to the Ryazan refinery feeding Moscow and Russian media reported repeated closures of all four Moscow airports through mid-October. Air travel is unreliable, and Western nationals face arbitrary detention on espionage or sabotage pretexts, with the FSB announcing the arrest of a Swedish national and a Japanese journalist in the same week; the 21 October release of American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff's talks with Putin shows detainees are treated as diplomatic currency. Western companies should treat Russia as no-go for travel; remaining staff need independent exit plans via Finland or the Baltics, noting Finland's land border is closed to civilian crossing.
BRIEF.TR: No terrorist attack or mass-casualty security incident was recorded in Türkiye in the 7-21 October window; the operational picture was dominated by the 14 October Istanbul flood disaster (eight confirmed dead per AFP on 19 October, roughly 2,000 homes and 900 businesses seriously damaged) and by the deepening political crackdown, with the Halk TV seizure on 14 October, further detentions of opposition mayors in Adana's Cukurova (19 October) and Milas (20 October) corruption probes, and jailed Istanbul mayor Imamoglu's defence under way. The PKK peace process continues to hold, with Reuters confirming the group's withdrawal from four Metina camps from 8 October, while Defence Minister Guler said on 20 October that Turkish troops would stay in Iraq and Syria until border security is assured; counter-terror policing remains active, with 14 suspected ISIS financiers detained in Ankara-led raids on 20 October following a German embassy tip. Iran-war spillover has not recurred since March; November's COP31 and the Imamoglu trial calendar raise the likelihood of demonstrations and heavy policing in Istanbul and Ankara.
BRIEF.IQ: The Kurdistan Region remains the most active theatre: Iranian drone and missile strikes on Iranian-Kurdish opposition camps in Erbil province were reported on 8, 12, 17 and 21 October (Reuters confirmed the 21 October missile strike north-east of Erbil), none causing reported casualties but all unanswered since coalition air defences left with the 30 September US withdrawal, and on 20 October Tehran's ambassador claimed Baghdad had agreed to expel or hand over the groups, a claim Iraqi officials have not confirmed and the KDPI rejects. Baghdad saw no attack on Western interests in-window, but the 17 October PMF depot explosion killed one and wounded four, a roadside bomb killed an army brigadier and a soldier near Kirkuk on 14 October in the second Islamic State-linked attack there this month, and Baghdad closed the Sheeb crossing with Iran on 21 October to review security. The US Mission issued a heightened-vigilance security alert on 18 October warning of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures; Erbil and Sulaimaniyah commercial flights continue, but the trajectory in Erbil province is toward more frequent strikes rather than fewer.
BRIEF.MA: Morocco recorded no security incident in the 7–21 October window that could be confirmed by a wire service; the only candidate item, a 12 October gathering in Rabat for hunger-striking Gdeim Izik prisoners that police dispersed, is reported by NGO and Moroccan sources only and is not carried in the feed. The operating environment is political rather than kinetic: the Ceuta migration dispute with Spain (King's 9 October speech, Spanish royal visit to Ceuta on 13 October, Reuters reporting on 19 October on Spain's rush to clear the Ceuta backlog), Algeria's 11 October announcement of 61 Moroccans arrested for alleged sabotage plans, and the UN Security Council's MINURSO renewal vote on 31 October may each generate rhetoric and small demonstrations but are unlikely to affect travel to major cities. A new coalition government under Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri was agreed on 12 October (Reuters). The last notable kinetic incident remains the Polisario rocket attack near Smara on 5 May (one civilian injured, older).
BRIEF.DZ: No terrorist attack, clash or significant protest was confirmed in Algeria for 7–21 October; the environment is stable but heavily securitised and the state continues to frame domestic problems (summer wildfires, migration networks) as foreign-backed subversion. The one confirmed development is the DGSN's 11 October announcement that 61 Moroccan nationals were arrested in Oran for allegedly preparing sabotage (Le Monde/AFP), which sharpens the Algiers–Rabat confrontation three weeks before the 31 October MINURSO vote; Spain's postponement of the 20–21 October Algiers summit and the September rupture with the UAE (airspace closure, Sky News Arabia accreditation withdrawn) underline a more combative foreign posture. The jihadist threat is low but not zero (failed suicide attack near a Blida police station in April and army–militant clashes in Tebessa in March, both older); the Sahel border belt and the far south remain off-limits for routine corporate travel.
BRIEF.TN: Tunisia's security risk is political rather than kinetic: the 17 October UGTT march was the largest show of opposition to President Saied in years and passed peacefully under heavy policing, but Reuters described it as a rare show of unity across the opposition against a backdrop of water and power cuts, medicine shortages and the detention of government critics (journalist Zied El Heni faced a further terrorism-charge hearing on 16 October). No terrorist incident or violent unrest was found in the window and nothing new was confirmed for 18–21 October. Expect further protests and possible strike action around central Tunis as the UGTT tests its leverage; interior and southern border areas (Chaambi, Libyan frontier) remain restricted.
BRIEF.EG: No terrorist attack, Sinai incident or domestic unrest was found in Egypt for 7–21 October, but two developments raise the external-security profile: the 10 October air strike on artisanal gold miners at Jabal al-Uqaydat on the disputed Sudan border (at least 72 dead per Sudanese rights monitors; Egypt's army says it is conducting a sovereignty campaign against illegal mining within its territory) and Cairo's pledge of 'all necessary and possible' support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, with a two-thirds parliamentary vote on authorising deployment now set for 26 October (Reuters). A deployment would expose Egypt to Houthi retaliation threats and keep Red Sea/Suez traffic, which had been recovering through mid-2026, at risk; Egypt–Sudan friction (truck drivers killed in Khartoum, Qustul freight crossings suspended) adds a southern dimension. North Sinai remains a restricted military zone and the entire Sudan border belt should be treated as no-go; Cairo, Alexandria, the Canal cities and Red Sea resorts remain workable with standard precautions.
BRIEF.LY: Libya remains Critical: the 18 October Zawiya mortar blast (at least nine security personnel dead, Reuters) shows how militia and security-force camps embedded in populated areas generate casualties even without active fighting, while UNSMIL's 9 October statement on enforced disappearances in Tripoli and Ghat confirms the kidnap and arbitrary-detention threat to foreigners. No large-scale Tripoli militia battle was wire-confirmed in-window, and SRSG Tetteh told the Security Council on 14 October that the political process had made 'encouraging progress' while urging it to 'hold spoilers accountable'; the east–west rapprochement over Türkiye (HoR vote 20 October, new speaker elected 6 October) marginally lowers the risk of a renewed national split while raising friction with Greece and Egypt. UNSMIL's mandate expires 31 October and renewal is expected. Earlier 2026 drone strikes on the Zawiya refinery (August), the Sharara–Zawiya pipeline shutdown (September) and the car-bomb killing of the LNA intelligence chief in Benghazi (10 August) show the baseline of targeted violence and infrastructure disruption.
BRIEF.NG: The north-east remains in its most dangerous phase in years: Boko Haram/ISWAP overran the Guzamala base on 13 October (at least 10 soldiers killed per Reuters) and killed 10 soldiers and five CJTF in a mine-and-ambush attack on a patrol near Gamboru Ngala on 17 October, despite military claims of more than 100 militants killed in airstrikes. In the north-west, bandits ambushed a military-escorted traders' convoy in Bukkuyum, Zamfara, on 10 October, killing at least 20 including eight security personnel, confirming that armed escort does not neutralise the threat on rural roads; kidnap-for-ransom persists on the Abuja–Kaduna axis and in Kaduna's peri-urban estates. New since 20 October is a confirmed Ebola (Bundibugyo) case in Abuja with 44 contacts under tracing, mostly healthcare workers: no travel restriction yet, but travellers should expect airport screening, avoid non-essential private-clinic use in the FCT and confirm medical-evacuation cover. Lagos and the south saw no major security incident in the reporting window.
BRIEF.NE: The first confirmed mass-casualty attack of the window struck the north rather than the jihadist-hit west: gunmen ambushed two escorted passenger buses on the Arlit–Agadez road on 20 October, killing at least 11 (AFP), on the only road corridor used by mining and humanitarian traffic between Agadez and the uranium belt; whether bandits, gold-robbers or anti-junta rebels, the escort failed to prevent it. The civil picture is deteriorating in parallel: the nationwide petrol shortage reached Niamey on 18 October, a fuel export ban has been in force since 12 October and ground movement is increasingly unreliable. The most recent major jihadist incidents remain the late-September ISSP assaults in Tahoua and Tillabéri (50+ security personnel killed, Reuters 30 Sep) after the failed 29 August mutiny; frontline army frustration, Africa Corps dependence and the junta's purge of critics keep coup and reprisal risk elevated, and Western nationals should treat Niger as no-go absent state-level clearance.
BRIEF.ML: Mali is in open, multi-front war: JNIM has held the Bamako approaches under a renewed fuel blockade since late April and inflicted the heaviest losses on the army in years in September, while ISSP's killing of at least 48 civilians (local tolls 50–70+) in Daoussahak camps around Tagadayat, Ménaka, on 18–19 October, described by Reuters' sources as reprisal for killings of suspected informants by the MSA militia and Africa Corps, shows the IS affiliate escalating in the east and the cycle of atrocity and counter-atrocity tightening, even as ISSP and JNIM fight each other across the Burkina border. The junta's recapture of Kidal on 6 October is a morale win but the supply picture is unchanged, with fuel reaching Bamako only in escorted convoys. Human Rights Watch's 19 October report (Reuters) documents 94 civilians killed in 47 Malian/Africa Corps drone strikes between April and August, more than double a year earlier, sharpening reprisal risk against anyone associated with the state or its partners; all travel should be deferred.
BRIEF.SD: The war is in a drone-dominated phase in which both SAF and RSF strike markets, funerals, displacement camps, dams, power plants and airports far behind the front lines: the 18-19 October wave in West Kordofan, Nyala and Khartoum killed well over 100 by AFP's count, the army's 19 October strike on Abyei's Amiet market (at least 153 dead per local officials) shows it will hit RSF supply lines across the South Sudan border, and the UN reported a 20 October drone strike on the Tendelti power station in White Nile. RSF drones reached Khartoum airport on 19 October and forced flight cancellations, Kordofan and Blue Nile remain active ground fronts with a repelled RSF/SPLM-N assault near Damazin on 19 October, and army-held Port Sudan and the eastern dams remain within RSF drone range. With the humanitarian plan 43 percent funded and no de-escalation track beyond a French-backed dialogue initiative, there is no basis for any corporate travel.
BRIEF.SS: South Sudan is now absorbing direct spillover from Sudan's drone war: the 19 October Amiet market strike in Abyei, which a Sudanese officer told AP targeted RSF-bound fuel tankers, is the deadliest single incident in the country this year and signals that supply corridors through South Sudanese territory will be targeted again; Juba has summoned Sudan's ambassador but has no means to deter further strikes. Internally, the 9 October Rumbek fighting (71 dead per the caretaker government) shows how quickly intercommunal violence can engulf a state capital, and the 2018 peace deal is effectively dead with Machar still on trial for treason in Juba and the government dissolved ahead of a December election timetable observers doubt can be met. Juba itself is calmer but politically brittle; expect further flashpoints in Abyei, Lakes, Jonglei and Upper Nile as the dry season opens roads to military movement.
BRIEF.SO: Wire-confirmed reporting shows the South West State conflict has widened to the point where Laftagareen-aligned forces hold every major Bay town except Baidoa, including Buur Hakaba on the Mogadishu road, with Ethiopian AU troops standing aside; the federally backed administration announced a counter-offensive on 18 October and Laftagareen on 20 October demanded President Mohamud step aside, so a fight for Baidoa itself is now the base case. In Mogadishu the electoral commission's unilateral April–May 2027 timetable has been rejected by the opposition, Puntland and Jubaland, keeping the June-style risk of armed political confrontation in the capital alive, while no large al-Shabaab attack in the city was wire-confirmed in the window. Rating 4 and rising trend are retained; posture remains no-go outside the airport/Halane enclave, with the Mogadishu–Baidoa road and all of Bay and Bakool regions closed.
BRIEF.ET: Four weeks after the TPLF-led alliance's 23 September offensive, federal forces and the allied Tigray Peace Force hold Mekelle, Adigrat, Adwa, Axum and Shire, flights to Mekelle have resumed and Addis has installed a six-month caretaker administration, but the TPLF rejects it, has warned against movement around Tigray's airports and is contesting roads and supply lines in central Tigray, while AFP reports collapsed policing, looting and stabbings in Adigrat and continuing Eritrean presence around Zalambessa. The Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation has not escalated into open war: Eritrean units largely pulled back north after Ethiopian drone strikes, the US has eased Eritrea-related sanctions to keep channels open and Rubio pressed Abiy for de-escalation on 14 October, yet diplomatic ties remain severed, both capitals' war rhetoric is undiminished and Addis keeps troops on the border. Amhara remains an active Fano insurgency zone with roads north of Addis unsafe; Addis Ababa functions under a heavy security posture and the UN's resident coordinator called for a Tigray ceasefire on 20 October.
BRIEF.ER: Eritrea is reported to be a belligerent in the Tigray war: witnesses, a foreign security source and conflict monitors say 5,000-8,000 of its troops crossed through Zalambessa and reached Adigrat in early October, were hit by Ethiopian drones and have largely pulled back toward the border, with AFP reporting on 18 October that Eritrean soldiers remain in Zalambessa on the Ethiopian side while Asmara denies any incursion. Ethiopia has severed relations and keeps troops on the frontier, Abiy continues to assert Ethiopia's need for sea access, and duelling UNSC letters frame each side as the aggressor, so a cross-border escalation within weeks remains plausible even though US pressure, including eased sanctions intended to keep channels to Asmara open, has so far held both armies on their own side of the line. Internal reporting from Eritrea is almost nil; assume mobilisation, communications restrictions and no exit options if the border war widens.
BRIEF.DJ: No violent security incident was recorded inside Djibouti in the past 14 days; the only major event was the 9 October migrant shipwreck off Obock, one of the deadliest on record on the Eastern Route, against a backdrop of thousands of Yemeni refugees arriving at Obock and migrants stranded in the desert. The exposure is external: the Ethiopia-Djibouti corridor runs through Afar, where the TPLF offensive briefly threatened the Semera road in late September before federal forces regained ground, while Houthi control of Perim and Yemen's Red Sea coast keeps Camp Lemonnier and the port within missile and drone range and Houthi statements have threatened states supporting Saudi Arabia. Djibouti City and the ports operate normally; monitor corridor security in Afar, war-risk insurance premiums and any Houthi targeting of Red Sea shipping or foreign bases.
BRIEF.KE: Nairobi and the main business corridors are operating normally, but the risk picture has shifted in two weeks: an imported Bundibugyo Ebola case has produced a nine-case cluster of relatives and healthcare workers in the capital, with no community transmission reported and 134 of 135 contacts quarantined, and the US has moved Kenya to Level 3 while explicitly flagging kidnapping and carjacking. The al-Shabaab IED threat to security convoys persists along the Somali border, where Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, Lamu and Tana River remain US Level 4, with the Marsabit-Turkana strip on the Ethiopian border added over unrest. Protest risk is resurfacing rather than acute: the 14 October fuel price hike brought small cost-of-living demonstrations and arrests in Nairobi on Mashujaa Day, and with the 2027 election cycle starting, assume rapid escalation potential around any further price or tax trigger.
BRIEF.CD: The eastern war has entered a new political phase: on 12 October former president Joseph Kabila launched the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN) in Goma, replacing the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 alliance with M23 leaders Nangaa, Bisimwa and Makenga as his deputies and a declared aim of ending 'tyranny' by force (Reuters); government spokesman Muyaya told AFP on 16 October that Kabila had formalised an 'attack against the Republic', the African Union on 20 October warned against any seizure of power by force, and Congolese media and Africanews report a 15 October interior-ministry ban on the activities of Kabila's PPRD and 12 other parties (not confirmed by a wire outlet). Fighting continues in North and South Kivu according to local media, and local sources report an ADF raid on mining sites in Mambasa (Ituri) around 16 October that killed about ten civilians, but no battlefield incident in the window could be confirmed by a wire service; in Ituri, UN OCHA confirmed fighting around the Rhoe displacement site on 12 October (at least four civilians killed, health centre burned) and an attack near Pimbo on 13 October (four killed, National Road 27 closed), both disrupting the Ebola response, which Reuters reports has spread to an eighth province (North Ubangi, 18 October) with Kenya confirming eight imported cases. Goma, Bukavu, Uvira and all of North/South Kivu and Ituri remain no-go; Kinshasa is operable with advance planning but carries elevated risk of politically driven unrest, arbitrary detention of persons linked to opposition figures, and sudden restrictions, with the president due to address the nation this week.
BRIEF.BR: Brazil is four days from a polarised presidential runoff (Flávio Bolsonaro 47% vs Lula 45% in the 4 October first round; a bitter first debate on 18 October, per Reuters) in which public security is the dominant issue. Rio remains the operational concern: two lethal police shootings in nine days (11 and 19 October) occurred on or near arteries used by business travellers (Avenida Brasil, Avenida Ayrton Senna/Linha Amarela), and the state electoral court's 15 October request for federal troops describes faction and militia control of territory and polling areas across 15 metro municipalities. International wire coverage in the window is confined to the campaign; the 2 October US suspension of consular services over security concerns (Reuters/AP) predates the window but frames the election-period threat picture. No incident in the window targeted foreigners. Note: the three Rio incidents are confirmed through Agência Brasil, the federal public news agency carrying Military Police, Civil Police, TRE-RJ and state-government statements, not through an international wire.
BRIEF.CO: Under President Abelardo de la Espriella (in office since 7 August) the state is on the offensive and has cancelled peace talks with the remaining rebel groups (AP), and armed groups are answering with an intensifying campaign on the Cauca stretch of the Pan-American Highway: AP confirms a 9 October clash in Timbío in which FARC-dissident Carlos Patiño fighters killed an army sergeant, a 10 October ELN drone strike that killed a soldier in La Vega, and a 12 October car bomb at the El Bordo toll plaza that injured three civilians and closed the highway. On the Venezuelan border, AFP and the Defence Ministry confirm an 11 October air strike on a Frente 33 camp in Catatumbo that killed four including a 16-year-old, the fourth such raid of the new government. An army-reported ELN attack that killed a soldier in Arauquita on 17 October could not be wire-confirmed and is flagged; Reuters separately reports 14 dead in an illegal gold-mine collapse in Santa Bárbara de Iscuandé, Nariño, on 19 October (not a security event). Bogotá, Medellín and Cartagena recorded no significant reported attack in the period.
BRIEF.VE: Venezuela remains in a managed post-Maduro transition rather than a confrontation: since the January 2026 US operation that captured Maduro, the Rodríguez siblings' interim government has reopened the oil sector (oilfield hiring picking up, Reuters 19 Oct), released hundreds of political prisoners, and the US is progressively delisting senior chavistas, most recently National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez on 14 October (Reuters). A third round of US-sponsored government-opposition talks is under way in Caracas without Machado, whose leadership the PUD alliance reaffirmed on 18 October (Al Jazeera/AFP). No US military action, detention of a foreign national or deadly unrest was found in the 7-21 October window. The near-term flashpoint is Thursday 22 October, when Vente Venezuela has called nationwide marches (Caracas from Plaza Venezuela, 16:00) and the PSUV a counter-march on the same day, per EFE and local media; neither call was found in Reuters/AP/AFP, but travellers should stand off from all gatherings and plan for traffic disruption in central Caracas that afternoon.
